payload.rationale: This is a broad background-based estimate, not a forecast anchored to current mortgage-rate observations. Rates above 7% have occurred during the higher-rate 2020s, so the threshold is plausible, but it is elevated relative to most post-2008 experience. I place more weight on rates being below the threshold by September 2026, while allowing substantial probability that inflation, Treasury yields, or mortgage spreads keep borrowing costs high. That weighting is a transfer assumption, not supplied evidence about current conditions. The event requires Freddie Mac’s first published September 24 PMMS value to exceed 7.01%; with ordinary two-decimal reporting, 7.02% qualifies and 7.01% does not. The strongest reason my estimate could be too high is that rates may already be well below 7%, leaving little time for the weekly average to cross the threshold. The strongest reason it could be too low is that rates may already be above 7.01%, making persistence through the measurement week likely. Without the latest PMMS observations, both possibilities remain unresolved.
limitations: No outside evidence or current research was supplied.
The latest PMMS rate, Treasury yields, mortgage spreads, and monetary-policy developments are unknown.
The short time to publication would make current rate observations highly informative; this estimate instead relies on a broad historical prior.
The contract specifies Freddie Mac’s first published weekly national average, not a daily lender quote or a subsequently revised value.
